title: Was there a curse on King Tut's tomb?
summary: Josh and Chuck examine whether a curse was on King Tut's tomb (KV62) in the Valley of the Kings. They cover Tut's life and reputed traits (chariots, inbreeding, club foot, skull shape), the leading theories of his death (chariot accident, war wounds, murder by clubbing), what a CT scan revealed about his injuries, the discovery of the tomb by Howard Carter and financier Lord Carnarvon, the alleged early opening and looting, the supposed "mummy's curse" and deaths linked to the dig, the 1933 Georg Steindorff rebuttal, Mark Nelson's 2002 British Medical Journal study finding no curse effect on lifespan, and scientific explanations such as mold, fungi and toxic gases in sealed tombs. The episode ends with listener mail about a kidney donation and a foot-binding question.

segments.title: Opening banter and King Tut trivia
segments.summary: Hosts open with casual banter, mention a Discovery exhibit in Times Square, and trade facts about Tut: chariots, ostrich hunting, marriage to his sister, club foot speculation, skull shape, and alien-breeding claims from Erich von Daniken.

segments.title: Theories of Tut's death and CT scan findings
segments.summary: The leading theories for Tut's death are a chariot accident, war wounds, and murder by a blow to the head. A CT scan of the mummy found an impacted wisdom tooth, no signs of infection, a leg fracture shown to be pre-mortem, and a skull gap that was just unfused bone. Injury evidence is complicated by damage from earlier handling.

segments.title: Discovery of the tomb and the looting question
segments.summary: Tut's tomb was the first royal tomb found with vast riches. Hosts discuss KV62 versus later KV63 and the claim by Howard Carter that thieves breached the tomb in ancient times.

segments.title: Lord Carnarvon and the opening of the tomb
segments.summary: Financier Lord Carnarvon, in poor health, traveled quickly to Egypt. Accounts differ on whether the 1923 entry was a brief peek or a full entry with stolen objects. Carnarvon died of an infected mosquito bite after shaving, and Carter's pet canary died the day the tomb was opened.

segments.title: Origins of the curse legend and early debunking
segments.summary: The curse story is traced to press exaggeration and to sources like Joseph Smith's account of Akhenaten's curse and Louisa May Alcott's story. An inscription on the tomb is quoted in several versions. Deaths linked to the dig are listed, and Georg Steindorff's 1933 paper rejected the curse.

segments.title: Mark Nelson study and survival rates
segments.summary: Mark Nelson of Monash University, in a British Medical Journal paper, compared survival of 44 Westerners present at Tut's tomb. Exposed people lived about 28 years after exposure versus 28.9 years for unexposed, and mean age of death was about 70 versus 75. Hosts note the study's dating omissions but conclude there is no curse effect.

segments.title: Mold, fungi and toxic gases in tombs
segments.summary: Sealed tombs may hold bacteria, mold, fungi, and gases such as hydrogen sulfide, ammonia and methanal that build up through decomposition. Carter's air samples are discussed. A recent sealed-tomb test found mold and toxic gases but levels likely not lethal, and a German study found dangerous mold in all 40 mummies tested.

segments.title: Listener mail: kidney donation and foot binding
segments.summary: A listener named Dustin describes donating a kidney to a coworker after hearing the show's organ donation episode. Hosts offer a T-shirt and invite listener stories. A brief exchange on Chinese foot binding closes the mail segment.
